summary: Gives example SIP call flows for race conditions, which are tricky timing situations that are hard to handle correctly. It shows best practices with message details for user agents and proxy servers. This is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: When two people try to hang up or call at the same instant, things can get confused. This memo shows what happens, step by step, and how to handle it.

questions: what is a sip race condition
what is the moratorium state in sip
what happens when two sip re-invites cross
why is bye in the early state not recommended
subtitle: Worked SIP call flows that show what each phone should do when two messages cross in flight.

tldr.problem: In SIP, one side can send a message just as the other side changes the call's state, so the two ends briefly disagree. Implementations that guess differently end up interoperating badly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds a dialog state machine with extra internal states (Moratorium, Mortal and others), then walks through example call flows in which messages cross and shows the recommended response in each.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice document: it clarifies behavior from RFC 3261 and gives implementors shared examples, but says the flows must not be copied as-is.

today: RFC 5407 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 147) from December 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a set of illustrative examples that clarify RFC 3261 rather than a protocol of its own.

sections.title: Why Race Conditions Need Examples
sections.content:
RFC 5407 collects example call flows of race conditions in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). These arise from transitions in dialog state, mainly during session setup after an INVITE is sent. The call flows were developed in the design of a SIP IP communications network.

The goal is to clarify what a SIP User Agent (UA) should do when messages cross each other, so that implementations do not interpret the situation inconsistently and interoperability improves. The flows are based on SIP 2.0 from RFC 3261 with SDP usage from RFC 3264.

The RFC is explicit that it does not prescribe the flows exactly as drawn. They illustrate best practice, and implementors must not copy them as-is because extra annotations were added for explanation. The examples also simplify real messages: Call-IDs are often replicated, CSeq often begins at 1, and headers such as Accept and Allow are usually left out. The actors are Alice, Bob and Carol (user agents) and a proxy server.
sections.eli5: Sometimes two phones say something to each other at the very same time. This document shows examples so every maker's phone reacts the same way.

sections.title: The Dialog State Machine
sections.content:
A race condition occurs when the dialog state at the receiving side differs from the state at the sending side. For example, a caller (UAC) may send a CANCEL in the Early state just as the callee (UAS) moves toward Confirmed by sending a 200 OK.

To reason about this, the RFC splits the dialog states of RFC 3261 into finer internal ones. The state before a dialog exists is Preparative. The Confirmed state is split into Moratorium (a 2xx has been sent or received but the ACK has not) and Established. The Terminated state is split into Mortal and Morgue.

In the Mortal state, entered by sending or receiving a BYE, the UA MUST NOT send any new requests in the dialog, and only a BYE is accepted; other requests in the INVITE dialog usage get an error. The UA still keeps dialog information for internal processing. It moves to Morgue, where the dialog no longer exists, when the BYE transaction ends.

A CANCEL does not itself change dialog state. The callee ends the dialog by sending a 487 right after receiving it. A caller MAY send a BYE in the Early state, but this is not recommended: with forking it only ends the early dialog with one particular UA, whereas CANCEL ends them all.
sections.eli5: A phone call goes through stages, like a game with levels. The memo gives the in-between levels names, so it can say exactly which level each phone is on when messages collide.

sections.title: Races in the Moratorium State
sections.content:
The Moratorium state is the short window after the callee sends 200 OK to the initial INVITE and before the ACK arrives. Six examples show messages landing in that window.

  • Retransmitted INVITE. Provisional responses are lost, so the caller resends the INVITE just as the callee sends 200. The callee MUST handle it as a retransmission, not a new INVITE, because the INVITE server transaction is not terminated by the 200 (a correction reported in a Work in Progress at the time).
  • CANCEL. The caller sends CANCEL while the callee sends 200 to the INVITE. The 200 to the CANCEL only means it was received. Because the INVITE succeeded, the caller sends a BYE right away.
  • BYE in the Early state. The BYE still works even though the INVITE transaction ended, because BYE is sent to the dialog, not to the request. The caller still sends an ACK to complete the INVITE transaction.
  • re-INVITE, case 1. The ACK was lost and a re-INVITE arrives. The callee sends 200 to it, since the dialog is already established.
  • re-INVITE, case 2. The offer is in the 200 and the answer is in the lost ACK, so the callee has an offer pending and answers the re-INVITE with 491.
  • BYE in the Established state. The ACK is lost, the callee retransmits 200, and the caller has already sent BYE. The caller must not re-establish the session.

For the re-INVITE and BYE cases the RFC offers an implementation tip: the caller can delay the message for some period (2 seconds, perhaps) so its ACK has probably arrived. It expresses no preference on whether to wait.
sections.eli5: It is like saying 'hello' on the phone while the other person says 'hello' too, before either hears the other. The rules say who goes ahead and who waits so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Races in the Mortal State
sections.content:
Four more examples cover a UA that has already sent a BYE and so is Mortal.

  • Both sides send BYE. A UA in the Mortal state still answers a BYE with 200 OK. Since the dialog ends either way, other responses would also work.
  • re-INVITE crossing a BYE. The re-INVITE gets a 481 because the receiver already sent BYE. The sender still sends an ACK for the 481, because that ACK belongs to the transaction layer.
  • 200 OK for a re-INVITE arriving after the UA sent BYE. The UA sends the ACK to complete the INVITE transaction while in the Mortal state. A tip: the UAC can delay the BYE until the re-INVITE transaction completes.
  • ACK arriving at a UA that sent BYE. When the offer is in the 2xx and the answer in the ACK, no session starts, and the answer in the ACK is ignored.

Dialog and transaction behavior are independent. A dialog can be terminated while a transaction is still running, so transaction handling continues in the Mortal state.
sections.eli5: If you have already hung up, you should not start a new chat. But you should still politely finish any handshake that was already underway.

sections.title: Crossing Requests and REFER
sections.content:
Three further examples are not tied to a dialog state change but to sessions.

Re-INVITE crossover. If both sides send re-INVITEs at once, each gets a 491 and retries after a different delay, as in RFC 3261. The UA that generated the Call-ID retries after 2.1-4.0 seconds; the other retries after 0.0-2.0 seconds. So every UA must remember whether it generated the Call-ID of the dialog. A UA should also decide whether a retry is still needed. For example, a hold crossing a request to add video could otherwise send video right after the audio is held.

UPDATE and re-INVITE crossover. If the UPDATE carries an SDP offer, both requests fail with 491. If an UPDATE for session refresh has no session description, both succeed with 200. The 491 is used because an SDP offer is pending.

REFER while Mortal. Bob sends REFER as Alice sends BYE. Alice, in the Mortal state, returns an error to the REFER. But Bob has already started a subscription usage with the REFER, so the dialog continues until that usage ends, and Bob follows RFC 5057.
sections.eli5: If you and a friend both shout 'my turn!' you each wait a different amount of time and try again. Whoever started the game waits a bit longer, so you do not collide again.

sections.title: Appendix Notes: BYE, CANCEL, Mortal and Forking
sections.content:
The appendices explain the reasoning behind the examples.

  • BYE in the early dialog (A). With a forking proxy, a BYE ends the dialog with one UA only, and the caller may still receive a final response such as 200 from another. So the caller MUST be prepared for a new dialog until the INVITE transaction ends. Use CANCEL to abandon the whole call attempt and BYE to abandon one early dialog.
  • BYE overlapping a re-INVITE (B). This is not a race. It describes what happens when there is no response to the re-INVITE; the UAS, on receiving the re-sent INVITE in the Mortal state, answers with an error such as 481 or 500.
  • CANCEL (C). In the Early state the callee sends 487 and the dialog terminates. In the Confirmed state no dialog change occurs, as the final response was already sent.
  • Mortal state (D). A 2xx received in the Mortal state extends the dialog usage to 64*T1 seconds to cope with 2xx retransmissions. BYE authentication with 401 or 407 is still processed.
  • Forking (E). Multiple 1xx responses with different To tags fork the state machine, and a 2xx for one early dialog terminates the others.
sections.eli5: The back of the memo explains why each rule exists, like a teacher showing the reasoning behind a game rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no new security rules. It contains clarifications of behavior specified in RFC 3261, RFC 3264 and RFC 3515, and the security considerations of those documents continue to apply after the clarifications are applied.
sections.eli5: This memo only explains how to follow rules that already exist, so the old safety rules still apply.
